question: What did Acme Logistics say about their current workflow?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract everything the Acme Logistics prospect said about their current workflow, including how work is done today, tools and systems currently used, pain points, bottlenecks, and any manual steps.
assumptions: 'Acme Logistics' matches the catalogue entry exactly (CALL-001), so no fuzzy mapping was needed.
'Current workflow' is interpreted broadly to include current processes, tools, and pain points.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: All of that is managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders. So renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late.
findings.context: Handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late. — Rachel describing current state in response to Maya asking for a concrete example of pain.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Sometimes a week. Sometimes we find out at the QBR
findings.context: Late-noticed issues can go unnoticed for about a week, and sometimes are only found at the QBR. — Rachel quantifying how late 'late' is.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something runs, then nothing happens for four days, then a human notices.
findings.context: Acme has some automation, but the main problem is the gaps between automated pieces, where work stalls until a human notices. — Rachel correcting the assumption that every step is manual.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed
findings.context: Acme's operational telemetry is weak: they can tell after the fact that something was late but cannot explain why, which dependency failed, or whether it recurs. — Rachel on measurement; outcome metrics exist but process telemetry does not.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: When something sticks, the escalation path depends entirely on who happens to see it. And people compensate — they build their own reminders, their own little spreadsheets, someone wrote a script once.
findings.context: Acme has no clear owner for automation; when something stalls, escalation depends on who happens to see it, and staff build their own reminders and spreadsheets. — Tom describing the informal workarounds around existing automation.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We have at least two scripts running that I could not tell you the author of.
findings.context: Acme runs at least three scripts whose authors nobody can identify, creating key-person risk. — Rachel said two; Tom corrected to three. Both are customer statements.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.context: Acme runs three unowned scripts (corrected from Rachel's count of two). — Tom correcting Rachel's count of scripts.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: Earlier we described onboarding as standardised. That's what the deck says. In practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.
findings.context: Onboarding is described as standardised in the deck, but in practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions, so one workflow diagram is misleading. — Tom correcting an earlier statement made by Acme about process standardisation.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: Customer and commercial data, that's clear. Tasks and tickets, that's somewhere else. And then a lot of the actual context is in chat
findings.context: Customer and commercial data have a clear system of record, but tasks and tickets live elsewhere and much of the process context sits in chat. — Rachel answering Maya's question about the system of record for the process.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: The data team uses it for a handful of back-office integrations. It works. But RevOps finds it too technical, and Rachel doesn't want every workflow change to become an IT ticket.
findings.context: Acme already uses Workato for a handful of back-office integrations run by the data team; RevOps finds it too technical, and Rachel does not want every workflow change to become an IT ticket. — Tom describing existing automation tooling.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor
findings.context: Acme already has a Workato contract and the internal question is whether to expand it rather than add another vendor. — Rachel on the commercial context for the current stack.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: maybe some of what we're paying Gainsight for
findings.context: Acme pays Gainsight and Rachel considers replacing some of that spend as part of the ROI case. — Rachel on justifying cost against existing tools.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: We've got expensive people doing coordination work because the systems don't carry enough process context.
findings.context: Acme has expensive staff doing coordination work because its systems do not carry enough process context. — Rachel on the real cost driver, framed as consistency and speed rather than headcount.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: A script takes two days to write and then quietly eats a few hours every month forever.
findings.context: Acme's internal scripts cause ongoing hidden engineering maintenance cost, roughly a few hours a month. — Tom on engineering cost not captured in original estimates.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: We've had integrations die because someone renamed a field or added a picklist value, and the automation just — didn't say anything.
findings.context: Integrations have broken silently when source schemas changed, such as a renamed field or added picklist value. — Tom describing a failure mode of existing automation.

draft.answer: Acme Logistics (Rachel Morgan and Tom Alvarez) said handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success run on spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so problems are noticed late, sometimes a week or only at the QBR [C1][C2]. They have partial automation, but work stalls in the gaps, there is no clear owner, and unowned scripts and silent integration failures add risk [C3][C4][C5]. Their stack includes Workato, which RevOps finds too technical, and Gainsight [C6][C7]. Process context sits in chat, and Tom said onboarding is not truly standardised across regions [C8][C9].

claims.text: Rachel Morgan said handoffs between sales, onboarding and customer success are managed through spreadsheets and Slack reminders, so renewal risks and implementation blockers get noticed late.
Rachel said issues can go unnoticed for about a week, and sometimes are only found at the QBR.

Acme has automation in places, but the problem is the gaps between automated pieces, where work stalls (Rachel cited four days) until a human notices. Tom said there is no clear owner for automation, escalation depends on who sees the problem, and staff build their own reminders, spreadsheets and scripts.

Rachel said operational telemetry is weak: Acme can tell after the fact that something was late but not why, or which dependency failed. Tom said integrations have died silently when a field was renamed or a picklist value was added.

Acme runs three scripts whose authors nobody can identify (Rachel said at least two, Tom corrected to three), creating key-person risk. Tom said scripts quietly cost a few hours of maintenance a month each, and Rachel said expensive staff do coordination work because systems lack process context.

Acme already uses Workato for a handful of back-office integrations run by the data team. Tom said it works but RevOps finds it too technical, and Rachel does not want every workflow change to become an IT ticket. Rachel said the internal question is whether to expand the existing Workato contract rather than add another vendor.
Rachel said Acme pays for Gainsight and she considers replacing some of that spend as part of the ROI case.
Rachel said customer and commercial data have a clear system of record, but tasks and tickets live elsewhere and much of the context is in chat.
Tom said onboarding was described as standardised in the deck, but in practice EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.

conflicts.description: Rachel said at least two scripts have unknown authors; Tom corrected the count to three.
Acme earlier described onboarding as standardised (the deck), but Tom said EMEA and North America use different milestone definitions.
